passage: I was on the terrace at Kabir's birthday when I noticed Pema holding the same cup of lime soda for an hour. Two of the boys kept holding out a bottle. "Just one, don't be boring," one said, and the other laughed. Pema smiled, shook their head and said, "No, I'm good, thanks." The bottle came back twice more. Pema's smile got smaller and their eyes kept going to the stairs. I can't say what Pema was thinking. Around eleven, Pema said, "Early class tomorrow," picked up a bag and left without any fuss. Next day I saw Pema in the canteen with the quiz club, laughing loudly over tea. Nobody at that table asked about drinking. I took the empty chair and joined in. Varun

qa.q: What did Pema hold for an hour at the party?
qa.a: Pema held the same cup of lime soda for an hour.

qa.q: What might Pema have been feeling as the bottle came back twice more?
qa.a: Possibly torn and uneasy, since Pema's smile got smaller and Pema's eyes kept going to the stairs, though Varun says the inner state can't be known for sure.

qa.q: What could Pema do if friends keep pushing next time?
qa.a: Say a simple no, leave early as Pema did, and spend more time with people like the quiz club who don't pressure.

qa.q: How might the boys who offered the bottle have seen the moment?
qa.a: They may have thought they were joking and including Pema, without noticing that "don't be boring" felt like pressure.

grounding: Friends push a drink with 'don't be boring'; Pema says a simple no, leaves early and finds easy company.

passage: The power had gone out across the colony, so the only light in the flat was Alka's phone torch when she found the vape pods in Bhupen's jacket. "How long? How long has this been going on?" Her voice cracked on the last word. Bhupen's ears burned. "It's not a big deal, Mummy, everyone does—" "Don't say everyone!" She sat down hard on the bed, still holding the pods. Bhupen's first urge was to grab the door and slam it. Then Bhupen saw her hand shaking. "You're scared," Bhupen said slowly. "Yes," said Alka. "I am." Thunder rolled outside and neither spoke for a while. "I'll see a doctor with you," Bhupen said at last, "if you stop shouting." Alka nodded and wiped her eyes.

qa.q: Where did Alka find the vape pods?
qa.a: She found the vape pods in Bhupen's jacket.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling underneath her shouting?
qa.a: Fear: her voice cracked, her hand shook, and she answered "Yes, I am" when Bhupen said she was scared.

qa.q: What could happen next to keep this from turning into a fight again?
qa.a: Bhupen and Alka could book the doctor visit together and agree a simple plan, so the fear gets an outlet other than shouting.

qa.q: How might the moment feel to Alka when Bhupen names her fear instead of arguing?
qa.a: She may feel heard rather than fought, which makes it easier for her to calm down and stop shouting.

grounding: A parent finds the habit and shouts; the protagonist feels cornered, hears the fear in the anger and agrees to a plan.

passage: The bus broke down two stops early, so Ganga ran the last stretch and reached the clinic with four minutes to spare, out of breath and clutching a crumpled appointment slip. Inside, Dr Farhan asked, "What brings you in?" Ganga had rehearsed a line all week: "Just a bit of gaming, some late nights." The words sat in the air, only half true. Ganga's palms were damp. Then, quietly: "It's more than that. Some nights I play until the sun comes up. I missed two lab sessions." Dr Farhan nodded and wrote something down. "Thank you for telling me that. And if there's a slip next week, come back anyway." Ganga's shoulders dropped for the first time that day, and a shaky laugh came out.

qa.q: Why did Ganga have to run to the clinic?
qa.a: The bus broke down two stops early.

qa.q: Why were Ganga's palms damp before speaking?
qa.a: Ganga was nervous about admitting the whole problem, and the rehearsed line was only half true.

qa.q: What would you advise Ganga to do if a slip happens next week?
qa.a: Go back to Dr Farhan anyway, as invited, and stay honest about what happened.

qa.q: How might Dr Farhan have seen Ganga's first answer compared with the second?
qa.a: The first gave only a softer half of the story, while the second gave the doctor the real picture to work with, and Dr Farhan answered with thanks.

grounding: The protagonist books an appointment nervous and relieved, and moves from a softened story to an honest one with the doctor.

passage:
Dear Elizabeth,
I went to the group on Thursday, the one I told you about. I sat by the door with my coat on for twenty minutes. Then a man in a green cap said, "Nobody here will judge you, we've all said worse." I cried a little and nobody rushed to fix me. Someone just passed tissues. I said out loud that I'd been drinking every night since March, and the room stayed warm. I walked home lighter than I've felt in months. I'm going back next week and I'll keep telling the truth there. But a part of me worries I could start needing their clapping more than my own steadiness, so I'll keep calling you too. Maybe one day I'll be the one passing tissues.
Love,
Salma

qa.q: How long did Salma sit by the door before someone spoke?
qa.a: Salma sat by the door with a coat on for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What is Salma worried about, even while feeling relieved?
qa.a: That the group's clapping could become more important than Salma's own steadiness, which is why Salma plans to keep calling Elizabeth too.

qa.q: What plans in the letter make this a healthy path?
qa.a: Going back next week, telling the truth there, staying in touch with Elizabeth, and maybe one day helping others as someone passing tissues.

qa.q: How might the man in the green cap have seen Salma's first visit?
qa.a: He probably recognised the nervousness from his own start, since he said everyone there has said worse, and wanted Salma to feel safe.

grounding: A support group accepts the protagonist without judgement, bringing relief and belonging, with a note of caution about depending only on approval.

passage: At 2 am, with the phone on four percent and an exam at nine, Kashish stared at the balance. Almost nothing left. The screen flashed, "So close! Double up and win it back!" Kashish's thumb hovered over a message to a classmate: "Can you lend me a bit till the first?" Then another bright offer popped up the second the last bet lost, a bonus that would expire in ten minutes. It's built to keep me here, Kashish thought. Every "so close" is bait. Kashish deleted the message unsent, switched on a blocker for every betting app, and shook Sachin's shoulder in the next bed. "I need to tell you something. I've lost my whole month's food money." Sachin sat up, blinking. "Okay. Tell me." The phone died mid-sentence, and it felt almost like relief.

qa.q: What time was it when Kashish stared at the balance?
qa.a: It was 2 am.

qa.q: What does Kashish think about the flashing "So close!" offers?
qa.a: Kashish grows wary and suspicious, seeing each "so close" as bait built to keep Kashish playing.

qa.q: What did Kashish do that was wise, and what could come next?
qa.a: Kashish blocked the betting apps, did not borrow, and told Sachin; next Kashish could ask a trusted adult or a counsellor for support with the gambling.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel about being woken with this news?
qa.a: Sachin may be surprised and sleepy, but the calm "Okay. Tell me." suggests wanting to help and being glad to be trusted.

grounding: The protagonist chases losses on a betting app at night, sees the game is built to keep them playing, blocks it and tells someone instead of borrowing.

passage: Zeynep had barely touched her tea in the dorm kitchen in Toronto, and Amara noticed. "I don't see the point of anything lately," Zeynep said to the table. "I've felt hopeless for weeks." Amara put her phone face down. She didn't say it would pass or tell her to cheer up. "Thank you for telling me. That sounds really heavy." Zeynep whispered, "Please don't tell anyone." Amara's heart pounded. "I can't promise to keep this secret if it means you're not safe. But I'll tell you before I tell anyone, and I'm not going anywhere." They sat until the tea went cold. In the morning Amara walked with Zeynep to the campus counselling centre and waited on the plastic chair outside the door.

qa.q: Where were Amara and Zeynep talking?
qa.a: They were in the dorm kitchen in Toronto.

qa.q: What did Amara want for Zeynep, judging by what Amara did the next morning?
qa.a: Amara wanted Zeynep to be safe and supported by a professional, shown by walking with Zeynep to the counselling centre and waiting outside.

qa.q: What could Amara do if Zeynep stops going to the counsellor?
qa.a: Keep checking in and staying close, and gently help Zeynep return, or reach a doctor or helpline.

qa.q: How might Zeynep have felt hearing that Amara couldn't promise secrecy?
qa.a: Perhaps worried or exposed at first, but the promise to tell Zeynep first and to stay probably made it feel less like betrayal.

grounding: A friend says she feels hopeless; the protagonist listens, takes it seriously, refuses secrecy and stays while helping her reach a counsellor.

passage: Warden's note, Thursday. Yusuf came to my office after dinner and stood at the door a while before sitting. Yusuf said a friend, Abhinav, has been skipping meals in the mess and keeping his door shut, and that Yusuf had stayed away for a week because "whatever I say will come out wrong." Yusuf's hands were tight together and the voice was low. I thought Yusuf looked more frightened than uninterested. I said plain, warm words are usually enough, and we wrote three short sentences on a card: I am here. I care. Let us get help. Yusuf took the card to Abhinav's room and I waited in the corridor. Afterwards Yusuf told me Abhinav opened the door and they sat quietly together. I have asked Abhinav to see the college counsellor tomorrow.

qa.q: What three short sentences did Yusuf and the warden write on the card?
qa.a: They wrote: I am here. I care. Let us get help.

qa.q: What was Yusuf afraid of?
qa.a: Saying the wrong thing, because Yusuf said "whatever I say will come out wrong" and stayed away for a week.

qa.q: What could Yusuf do if Abhinav says little back?
qa.a: Keep showing up quietly, repeat the simple words, and help Abhinav reach the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have experienced Yusuf's week of staying away?
qa.a: Possibly as being left alone, which can feel like nobody cares, though the note only says Abhinav opened the door later and they sat together.

grounding: The protagonist fears saying the wrong thing to a struggling friend; simple warm words replace avoidance.

passage: Sonali had a practical exam in the morning when Saurabh's call lit up her phone at eleven for the third night running. She answered anyway. "I can't sleep, it's all pointless, tell me it's okay." She said the right words in a flat voice, then sat with her notes unread and her jaw tight. She resented him, quietly, and resenting him made her feel like a bad friend. The next afternoon she told the college counsellor everything, resentment included. The counsellor said tiredness like this was human and asked who else was around Saurabh. Sonali rang his older sister and his roommate. Then she told Saurabh gently, "I care about you, but I can't be the only one you call. I'll check in at six every evening." Saurabh was quiet, then said, "Okay."

qa.q: How many nights in a row had Saurabh called at eleven?
qa.a: It was the third night running.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel about herself for resenting Saurabh?
qa.a: Like a bad friend, guilty as well as worn out.

qa.q: What limits did Sonali set, and how do they help?
qa.a: She offered a check-in at six each evening instead of being the only person he calls, and brought in his sister and roommate, so the load is shared.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt hearing that Sonali cannot be the only one he calls?
qa.a: Possibly hurt or afraid of being left, which may be why he went quiet, but she also said she cares and offered a regular check-in.

grounding: The protagonist, exhausted as one friend's only support, resents him and shares the load with others while keeping her limits.

passage: Come, sit, Meera beta. You asked how to help a friend without disappearing yourself, so listen to Pooja's story. I was twenty. My friend Vasudha called me at two, at four, in the middle of lectures. I felt so important, beta, the only one she trusted. And so tired that I fell asleep on the bus. My mother said, "You are not her doctor." I was angry with Ma for a week. Then one night I said, "Vasudha, I love you, but I can't be your only support. Let's meet the college counsellor together, and call your sister too." She cried. I cried. I sat with her at the first appointment, but I stopped picking up every single call. It felt like betrayal then. It was also the first time she got real help.

qa.q: How old was Pooja when Vasudha started calling at all hours?
qa.a: Pooja was twenty.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel about being Vasudha's only support?
qa.a: Important and needed, yet so tired that Pooja fell asleep on the bus.

qa.q: What did Pooja do that joined care with limits?
qa.a: Pooja suggested going to the college counsellor together, urged Vasudha to call her sister, and stopped picking up every single call.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have felt when Pooja stopped answering every call?
qa.a: She may have feared being dropped, and she cried, but the change also led her to real help at the appointment.

grounding: An elder recalls a friend who relied on her for everything: needed and drained, she set limits and steered the friend toward professional help.

passage: You want to know if there is ever a time to break a promise, Rhea? I'll tell you one. I'm Nikita, and at twenty a friend of mine, Tanmay, sat beside me on the library steps and said he was in such deep pain he couldn't see a way through. "Promise you won't tell anyone," he said. My hands went cold. I wanted to say yes just to keep him talking. Instead I said, "I can't promise that. I care about you more than I care about the promise. But I'll tell you first, and I'll be right there with you." He was furious and didn't speak to me for two days. Then we went to the hostel warden together, and later to a doctor. Years on, he thanked me at his wedding.

qa.q: Where were Nikita and Tanmay sitting when Tanmay confided?
qa.a: They were sitting on the library steps.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel when Tanmay asked for a promise?
qa.a: Nikita's hands went cold with fear, and there was a wish to say yes just to keep Tanmay talking, yet Nikita cared more about Tanmay's safety than the promise.

qa.q: What did Nikita do that is worth copying?
qa.a: Nikita told Tanmay first, stayed with him, and went with him to the hostel warden and later a doctor.

qa.q: How might Tanmay have felt when Nikita would not promise?
qa.a: Furious and perhaps betrayed, since he did not speak to Nikita for two days, though years later he was thankful.

grounding: A friend confides deep pain and asks for secrecy; the protagonist puts safety over the promise, tells him first and involves a trusted adult and doctor.
